Pi, Luna, Chrome Control, and Automic Vault: Detailed Video Notes

Source video: L8 Principal Building a Full Stack App with Agentic Engineering — Kun Chen
Duration: 1:40:02 · Notes prepared: 20 September 2026 · Language: English

Kun builds Eddie’s Wallet, a virtual allowance and financial-learning app for his family, using a team of agents coordinated through Firstmate. The coding agents run Pi with GPT-5.6-Luna at xhigh reasoning. He handles product decisions, reviews interactive plans, and verifies the finished experience while the agents research, implement, configure infrastructure, and repair integration problems.

The two especially useful parts are letting Pi operate an already signed-in Chrome session and letting agents use production credentials through Automic Vault. Together, these let an agent move beyond generating code into doing the operational work needed to make an application function.

Name correction: the product is Automic Vault, confirmed in the video screenshots and its official repository. The automatic captions often say “Atomic Vault.” It is a secrets manager, rather than a notes or knowledge vault. “Chrome DevTools XE” in the captions refers to chrome-devtools-axi.

Evidence guide: the video sections below summarize the full English automatic-caption track, checked against selected screenshots. Sections marked Practical supplement use current primary documentation and are not a literal reconstruction of every command Kun ran. Model performance, pricing, quota behavior, and compaction comparisons described by Kun are observations from his recording, not guarantees for a current account. The design work also uses Claude Design with Sonnet, so the entire workflow is not exclusively Luna.

1. What each part of the setup does

Component Role in this workflow
Luna The model that interprets instructions, reasons, and decides which actions to take
Pi The agent harness that runs the model and executes its tool calls
Firstmate The coordination layer: the human talks to one agent, which assigns and supervises work
Herdr The terminal environment that makes the separate agent sessions visible and accessible
chrome-devtools-axi The command-line browser interface available to the agent
Chrome DevTools MCP / Chrome The underlying browser-control capability and the browser session being operated
Automic Vault The separate authorization and delivery mechanism for secrets used by commands
Pi Launcher The signed macOS launcher shown as the requesting application in the vault dialog
Lavish Interactive HTML plans, diagrams, annotations, and prototypes for human review
Claude Design Design-system and visual-design work before the native frontend is implemented

This separation matters. Selecting Luna in Pi does not, on its own, connect a browser or configure a vault. Those capabilities come from the surrounding tools and setup. Likewise, Firstmate is useful for managing multiple workstreams, but a single Pi agent can use a browser CLI without adopting the whole team workflow.

2. Deep dive: controlling an existing Chrome session with Pi and Luna

What Kun actually delegates

Around 1:10–1:13, Firstmate identifies Apple Developer configuration that is still required. Kun initially asks for the exact steps and URLs so he can do them himself. He then changes the approach: he tells Firstmate that it can use chrome-devtools-axi to control his browser and that he has already signed in to Apple’s service.

The agent navigates the Apple setup flow, works with the application identity, and registers the app with the required Sign in with Apple capability. Kun can see it manipulating the browser while other work continues.

The relevant shift is from “tell me which buttons to click” to “perform the authorized setup in the browser I already use.” The session already carries his login state, so the agent does not need him to paste his Apple password into the conversation.

Why the existing browser matters

At 1:19:18–1:20:03, Kun explains that he enabled Chrome’s remote debugging before recording. Without that connection, the automation would use a separate browser instance, which would not necessarily contain his authenticated session.

He also explains that a new agent connection prompts for permission. The recording shows remote debugging enabled and a server address of 127.0.0.1:9222.

“Remote” here means an external program controls Chrome through its debugging interface. This video demonstrates that on Kun’s own computer. It does not demonstrate a second laptop controlling Chrome across a network, an SSH tunnel, or a VPN connection.

What the browser interface provides

Practical supplement. The current AXI tool wraps Chrome DevTools MCP in a CLI. It provides navigation, accessibility snapshots, element actions, screenshots, JavaScript evaluation, and console/network inspection. A persistent bridge keeps browser state available across command invocations. The agent can use page structure to choose controls, then inspect the resulting state. Official AXI documentation

That creates a useful feedback loop:

  1. Inspect the current page and identify the relevant control.
  2. Perform an action, such as filling a field or clicking a button.
  3. Read the resulting page, including validation errors.
  4. Verify the intended outcome before continuing or reporting success.

This is particularly relevant to work such as configuring a developer portal, inspecting a dashboard, or following a multi-step administrative UI.

The failure in the demo is worth studying

The first registration attempt does not succeed. At 1:15–1:18, Kun sees a problem with the application’s display name. Later, Firstmate reports that the App ID has not appeared. Kun points out that the name may contain unsupported characters and asks it to try again.

The retry succeeds, and the app is registered at about 1:19:05.

The lesson is that browser access and reliable task completion are separate things. Luna can operate the UI, yet still miss a validation message or fail to connect it to an unsuccessful operation. A good task definition includes the observable final state: the new App ID must appear, with the intended capability enabled.

Practical supplement: the smallest setup to reproduce the connection

These steps are based on current documentation. They have not been executed on your Mac.

A. Enable the connection in Chrome. In Chrome 144 or newer, open:

chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging

Enable remote debugging and keep Chrome running. Chrome presents a permission dialog when the tool connects. With multiple active profiles, automatic connection uses the default profile selected by Chrome and can access that profile’s open windows. Confirm that this is the profile you intend to use. Chrome’s advanced usage guide

B. Make the CLI available and select existing-browser mode. With Node.js/npm and Pi already installed:

export CHROME_DEVTOOLS_AXI_AUTO_CONNECT=1
npx -y chrome-devtools-axi pages

Approve Chrome’s connection prompt, then start Pi from that terminal so it inherits the setting. If an AXI bridge was already running in a different mode, stop it before reconnecting:

npx -y chrome-devtools-axi stop

The optional skill installation documented by the author is:

npx skills add kunchenguid/chrome-devtools-axi --skill chrome-devtools-axi -g

Check that the installer targets Pi and that Pi discovers the skill. The CLI can also be invoked directly without installing a skill. AXI setup and configuration

C. Select your model in Pi. Use /model to select the available Luna entry, and /thinking to select the desired supported reasoning level. The video uses xhigh. Availability depends on the provider/account configured in your Pi installation. Pi documentation

D. Start with a bounded inspection task. Suggested prompt, written for these notes:

Use chrome-devtools-axi to inspect my existing Chrome session.
List the open tabs and identify the one for [target website].
Read that page and summarize the current setup status.
For this first check, do not change any settings.
If the expected tab is missing or Chrome needs connection approval,
tell me what you observed.

For a later action task, specify the desired change and its verification condition. For example: “Enable this capability for this test app, then reopen its details and confirm the capability is enabled.”

Applying this to a browser on another computer

Practical supplement, beyond the video. The direct lesson is to first establish the local Pi-to-Chrome connection. A two-computer arrangement additionally needs a reachable browser endpoint and an appropriate connection boundary. AXI supports explicit HTTP or WebSocket browser endpoints, but the video does not provide a complete cross-machine recipe. AXI connection configuration

For a company portal, browser connectivity, VPN routing, logged-in identity, and account permissions are separate requirements. A successful connection to Chrome does not expand the privileges of the account signed in to the site. It is useful to verify those layers individually before adding unattended actions.

3. Deep dive: Automic Vault and agent access to secrets

What it solves in this demo

At 59:41–1:00:38, Kun starts backend work while the design system is being prepared. The agents need to manage Hetzner infrastructure. He says the required token is already in his vault and gives the agent its name, HCLOUD_TOKEN.

When the agent requests its use, Automic Vault displays a separate approval window. Kun can inspect the command before allowing it. He chooses individual approvals because he wants to observe the operations against his account during this session.

This screenshot makes the arrangement concrete. The dialog identifies Pi Launcher, shows a shell command that checks whether HCLOUD_TOKEN is present, lists the working directory and required key, and offers Deny and Approve Once. The token’s value is not displayed.

The sequence to understand

  1. The user stores a credential in the vault. In the video, the credentials are already present; their initial import is not demonstrated.
  2. The agent is told the secret’s name and the authorized purpose. For example, use HCLOUD_TOKEN to configure the app’s Hetzner infrastructure.
  3. The agent proposes a command that needs that secret. The vault mediates the request.
  4. The user inspects and approves or denies it. Kun looks at the proposed command and requesting application.
  5. The approved process receives the secret and performs the operation. The model can receive useful results without the user pasting the raw credential into the chat.

The “automatic” part is that the agent can request and use credentials as part of its workflow. It does not mean every request is silently allowed. Kun explicitly declines blanket approval during the demonstrated Hetzner work.

The second example: Cloudflare and DNS

At 1:24–1:27, the agents need a hostname and HTTPS to connect the iOS app to the deployed backend. Kun gives them a domain he controls and says a Cloudflare credential exists in the same vault.

He initially gives the wrong credential name. He checks the vault and corrects it to CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, in uppercase. The agent then obtains approval to use it. Firstmate subsequently reports that the backend is live at the intended address with valid HTTPS.

There are two distinct recovery cases here. The agent resolves a spelling mistake in the intended hostname from context, but a missing vault entry still needs the exact stored name. A credential name is an identifier that must match, not a description the system can always infer.

What “the agent never sees the token” means

At about 1:27, Kun explains that the token is passed as an environment variable for the command to use, rather than being exposed in ordinary chat output.

The useful interpretation is reduced exposure to the model transcript. It is not a claim that the receiving process cannot access the token. A program supplied with an environment variable can read it; whether it logs or transmits that value depends on the program and operation.

Current Automic Vault documentation explicitly places the boundary at credential handoff: the destination program controls the secret after receiving it. That is why the command and destination matter as well as the requesting agent’s identity. Automic Vault documentation

Pi Launcher is a separate piece

The approval window says Pi Launcher, rather than merely showing a generic shell. Kun’s separate Pi Launcher project provides a signed macOS launcher for Pi. This is relevant to the vault’s ability to identify the requesting application. It is not a Chrome extension, a model, or a replacement for Pi. Pi Launcher project

The video does not walk through installing and enrolling it. Do not assume that a plain Node-based Pi installation will display the same identity in every macOS authorization system.

Practical supplement: getting started with the current vault

The official macOS installation command is:

brew install --cask automic-vault/isotopes/automic-vault

Open Automic Vault and follow its setup. Current documentation supports migrating credentials from supported tools, saving named secrets, and authorizing their use. For example:

av save HCLOUD_TOKEN
av save CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN

Enter the values through the prompted input. The documented low-level injection form is av inject +SECRET_NAME -- /path/to/program; the project recommends its supported tool integrations or reviewed scripts where appropriate. Official installation and secrets guide

Start by verifying one harmless read operation against a test resource. Confirm the requesting application, intended command, requested secret name, and returned result. Only then expand the workflow to the specific changes you want the agent to perform.

Browser permission and vault permission cover different things

Permission What it enables What it does not establish
Chrome debugging connection The tool can inspect and operate the connected browser profile That a particular click succeeded, or that every possible action is intended
Vault authorization An approved operation can receive or use the required credential That the operation is correct, or that the receiving program cannot misuse the credential
Task authorization from the user The agent has a defined goal and scope That the resulting application has actually been verified

A signed-in browser can already perform account actions through its existing session. Those actions do not inherently require a new Automic Vault request. The two permission flows complement each other; the vault is not a universal approval gate around all browser actions.

4. The full development workflow, with the key decisions preserved

00:00–05:41: establish the team and reduce interface noise

Kun starts with his development tools already configured, clones Firstmate, and launches Pi in its directory. He changes from his usual Sol model to Luna and instructs Firstmate to use Luna at xhigh for every crewmate in this demo.

Herdr exposes the worker sessions as normal, inspectable terminal sessions. Firstmate becomes the main conversational contact, handling assignment, status, follow-up instructions, and cleanup.

He enables /calm to hide the stream of tool activity from the main view. In the video, he describes this as a Pi-specific Firstmate feature. Its purpose is to reduce what the human must watch; it is not evidence that tool calls or model context have disappeared.

05:41–19:06: product intent, market research, and technical research

The app starts from a real family problem: allowance rules and balances are scattered between memory and a notebook. Kun wants a virtual ledger plus understandable lessons about balances, borrowing, repayment, and interest.

The initial constraints include:

  • Virtual money, with no real banking integration.
  • iOS/iPad usage first, with data available across devices.
  • Parent-controlled changes and a child view that is initially read-only.
  • Cloud persistence so the parent’s phone and child’s iPad can share the data.

Firstmate sends market research and technical research to different workers. The market report claims it found no exact match for the full brief, which Kun accepts as a reason to prototype. That is a research result within the demo, not proof that the market is empty or that demand is validated.

Other product ideas include an activity timeline, recurring allowance rules, contextual lessons, and simulated loans. Kun is cautious about manipulative gamification and does not want ads driving the experience.

13:17: optional fast mode and quota visibility

Kun uses a Pi extension to enable a Codex fast mode for the recording. He observes that the setting appears enabled in another worker session too. He describes a latency-versus-consumption trade-off and normally leaves it off.

A separate menu-bar widget displays subscription quota information. These are details of his configured environment. The recording does not establish a universal billing rule for every Pi login, and the displayed token/cost information should not be read as your invoice.

19:06–42:29: make technical trade-offs visible

The first technical recommendation includes SwiftUI, Supabase, PostgreSQL authorization, a server-side ledger, and local caching. Kun challenges the hosted-backend choice because the initial users are his family.

He asks for a Lavish artifact so he can inspect options, diagrams, and open decisions and annotate particular elements. While backend planning proceeds, another worker explores frontend flows.

The initial cost comparison puts self-hosted infrastructure much higher than Kun expects. He challenges the estimate and asks for evidence about low-cost Hetzner options. The revised proposal is closer to the roughly five-dollar monthly level he had in mind. These amounts belong to the video’s comparison and are not current quotations.

He also removes premature audit/export requirements, chooses a parent-managed child profile with a PIN gate for parent actions, and keeps recovery requirements proportionate to this MVP. The important intervention is correcting the assumptions behind the recommendation, rather than accepting the first polished-looking plan.

42:29–48:08: test the user flow before polishing it

One worker initially produces a written prototype scope instead of a playable prototype. Kun clarifies that he wants an interactive HTML wireframe in Lavish, without needing to build the native iOS app yet.

He walks through family setup, device pairing, child view, parent mode, allowances, and loans. His feedback includes using a familiar local currency, avoiding duplicate recent-activity navigation, and keeping point requests as an in-person conversation with parents rather than an app feature.

He then asks the agent to capture the decisions in the repository’s README as a PRD. The interactive artifact helps him discover what he wants; the document preserves what was decided.

48:08–55:36: preserve context and establish the repository workflow

Kun discusses an extension that makes Pi use OpenAI server-side compaction. His claim is that this improves continuity in his long-running GPT sessions. Later, he also credits Firstmate’s persisted task files for retaining recoverable detail.

The transferable pattern is to combine conversation compaction with durable task state. A compressed conversation can point back to the PRD, decisions, reports, and work records when needed.

He publishes the app repository, fixes the spelling of Eddie across local and remote references, and moves from a local-only workflow to direct PRs. He explicitly permits reviewed PRs to merge autonomously for this early prototype. He defers his stronger No Mistakes validation pipeline until a stage where he would otherwise want peer review. These are his choices for this project, not required settings for Pi or Firstmate.

55:36–1:13:52: design and backend work proceed together

Kun gives Claude Design the repository containing the PRD and asks it to create a design system. A higher-end option is overloaded, so he proceeds with Sonnet.

He requests a design system to keep future screens consistent, then reviews colors, alignment, visual tone, sample flows, and icons. He pushes the design toward a more child-friendly experience and chooses a piggy-bank icon, asking for usable iOS assets.

Meanwhile, Firstmate starts backend, database/authentication, and infrastructure work. Kun uses Automic Vault for the Hetzner credential and asks for infrastructure to be declared with OpenTofu, so resources are represented as reviewable, version-controlled configuration.

1:13:52–1:20:33: build the frontend and configure Apple

Kun exports the design system as a ZIP and gives its local path to Firstmate. He asks it to copy the design assets into the repository and build a native app for iPhone and iPad.

He also decides that the backend should live in a private repository while the frontend remains public. At the same time, Firstmate operates his signed-in Chrome session to complete Apple configuration. This is where the invalid display-name failure and subsequent successful retry occur.

1:20:33–1:33:46: integration exposes the unfinished work

Firstmate reports merged work, a backend, and simulator validation. Kun asks whether the frontend is actually connected to the backend. It is still using a mock.

He supplies a stronger completion condition: sign in with his real Apple account in the simulator and use the actual backend running on the VPS.

The agents then work on real frontend authentication/integration and backend deployment, DNS, and HTTPS. Kun rejects separate development and production tiers for this particular family MVP. He supplies Cloudflare access through the vault and corrects the stored secret name.

Several remaining problems surface:

  • The frontend uses the wrong backend address because it was built while deployment details were still changing.
  • Apple sign-in fails during testing; the agents investigate rather than treating the first attempt as completion.
  • UI text assumes every child is named Eddie, confusing the product’s brand with the user’s name.

Firstmate assigns fixes and coordinates the changed information. This is a clear example of parallel work creating integration dependencies that still need active reconciliation.

Kun briefly mentions using Tailscale for future deployment connectivity, including VPS machines and potentially GitHub Actions runners. He does not configure that setup in this video.

1:33:46–1:40:02: review the architecture and prove the experience

While authentication debugging continues, Kun requests a Lavish architecture review focused on API endpoints, authentication, and database structure.

The review shows an HTTPS-facing Fastify API, authentication/session handling, wallet operations, and database entities such as parent identities, families, children, wallets, loans, and ledger entries. Kun checks whether those concepts and boundaries are reasonable and whether unnecessary complexity has appeared.

Finally, he signs in, adds $10 of virtual allowance, sees the balance in the child view, signs out, and signs back in. The data remains available. This verifies the demonstrated path through authentication, backend access, and persistence.

He plans to create a TestFlight build and install it on his son’s iPad afterward. The video shows a working simulator flow; it does not show completion of TestFlight distribution or exhaustive testing of every feature.

5. What makes this useful for your own Pi workflow

My synthesis, rather than a claim made verbatim in the video: the strongest idea is to provide an agent with three things together: a useful action interface, persistent task context, and an observable definition of success.

For Chrome work, the action interface is browser inspection and control. Persistent context is the target account, task, current progress, and any errors already encountered. Success is a verified state in the application, not merely the fact that a click command ran.

For API or infrastructure work, the action interface is a tool that can perform the intended operation. Automic Vault governs credential use. Success is the resulting resource, response, configuration, or working user journey.

For your own experiments, a sensible progression is:

  1. One Pi agent inspecting Chrome. Confirm the intended signed-in profile and tab are visible.
  2. One reversible browser action. Require read-back evidence of its result.
  3. One vault-mediated API read. Confirm the credential is usable without printing its value.
  4. One small integrated task. For example, inspect a test configuration in the browser and verify the corresponding API result.
  5. Add Firstmate when there are genuinely independent workstreams. Keep the final integrated outcome explicit.

Luna’s role in the demo is encouraging, but the work succeeds with substantial structure and human judgment. Kun corrects a cost assumption, clarifies prototype requirements, spots a browser error, fixes a secret identifier, and rejects a “finished” result that still uses mock data. Those interventions are part of the demonstrated workflow.

6. Reusable task brief for a local agent

The following is an original template based on the workflow, not a quotation from the video:

Goal:
Complete [specific task] using Pi and my existing Chrome session.

Model:
Use the available Luna model. Keep the selected model and reasoning
level visible, and report if the requested option is unavailable.

Browser:
Use chrome-devtools-axi to connect to the intended Chrome profile.
Confirm the target website and account before making changes.
After each meaningful action, inspect the result and any validation error.

Credentials:
Use Automic Vault for [exact secret names] only for [authorized purpose].
Let the vault present its approval requests. Keep secret values out of
chat, screenshots, generated documents, and ordinary command output.

Completion evidence:
[Observable outcome, for example: the test app appears with the required
capability enabled, and the corresponding API read returns that setting.]

Continuity:
Record the current task, confirmed facts, errors, and next action in a
local task note so work can resume after compaction or restart.

If blocked:
Describe the observed error and the next available step. Ask me to act
when the remaining step requires my identity, approval, or decision.
